item.title: Manufacturing Happy Hour: 306: From Systems of Record to Systems of Action: Putting AI to Work in Manufacturing with Sanjay Brahmawar
item.description:
Manufacturing has a lot to gain from AI, and a lot to lose by waiting.

Recorded at mHUB in Chicago’s West Loop during IMTS (International Manufacturing Technology Show), Chris sits down with Sanjay Brahmawar, CEO of QAD Redzone, to talk about what AI could mean for an industry facing 500,000 open manufacturing jobs and a growing need to do more with the people it already has.

They also look at what happens when systems of record become systems of action, and how that changes the way manufacturers respond to problems on the shop floor.

In this episode, find out:

  • How a career that started on a Honda engine line shaped Sanjay's view of manufacturing as managing constraints
  • Why manufacturers don't need to replace their existing technology before putting AI to work
  • How AI can turn a system of record into a system of action on the factory floor
  • What QAD Redzone learned after giving line leads an AI agent before bringing their supervisors into the conversation
  • Why some manufacturers are willing to set aside 5-7% of their IT budget for AI
  • How a month of 24/7 bug fixing, complete with its own t-shirts, helped QAD Redzone rebuild customer trust

Enjoying the show? Please leave us a review here. Even one sentence helps. It’s feedback from Manufacturing All-Stars like you that keeps us going!

Tweetable Quotes:

  • "The role of AI is not to replace the human being. The role of AI is to make that human being, that talent, 3 to 4x more powerful." - Sanjay Brahmawar, CEO of QAD Redzone
  • "Manufacturing is a show-me world. It is not a tell-me world." - Sanjay Brahmawar, CEO of QAD Redzone
  • "Nobody in manufacturing is sitting there waiting for somebody to give them AI. They only want it if it impacts their outcomes." - Sanjay Brahmawar, CEO of

item.title: NerdWallet's Smart Money Podcast: Splitting the Bill With Friends? Navigate Venmo Requests, Unpaid Loans and Money Regrets
item.description:
Learn how to handle money tension with friends and partners, from splitting costs to getting a loan paid back.
Is it fair for a friend to split every grocery bill with you when they earn far more than you do? Hosts Sean Pyles, CFP®, and Elizabeth Ayoola dig into some of Reddit’s messiest money conversations, with posts read by NerdWallet senior banking writer Spencer Tierney, credit expert Amanda Barroso and content strategist Jackie Tucker. You’ll hear why surprise payment app requests can sting, how rarely money values come up between friends, whether splitting every cost makes a friendship feel transactional, and what to consider when a friend borrows money twice and then asks whether they really need to pay it all back.
Then, how much money does it take to stop worrying about money? Sean and Elizabeth discuss why there may never be a magic number, how medical bills and rising health care costs feed financial anxiety, and what a viral article about Gen Z women paying for, and parenting, their boyfriends reveals about the difference between a wage gap and an effort gap in relationships. They also open up about the financial decisions they regret (or refuse to), from overstaying in a low-wage job market abroad to not setting money aside for taxes, and react to Redditors’ biggest regrets, including selling Microsoft stock in 1992 and skipping a prenup.

item.title: Filmspotting: "Hollywood's like Egypt, full of crumbled pyramids" with Laura Friedman & Ron Falzone | The Movie Racket
item.description:
Hollywood has been dying for more than a century. At least, that's what people keep saying.

This week, Michael Phillips explores one of the industry's favorite prophecies of doom: producer David O. Selznick's famous comparison of Hollywood to ancient Egypt, "full of crumbled pyramids" destined to disappear into the sands.

Joining Michael are Rep. Laura Friedman, whose congressional district includes many of the major studios and who helped author the bipartisan Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, and film historian Ron Falzone. Together, they examine Hollywood's latest existential crisis: runaway production, empty soundstages, corporate consolidation, and the fight to keep movie-making in the United States.

Is Hollywood facing a uniquely perilous moment, or just its latest near-death experience? Join the conversation by emailing themovieracket@filmspotting.net.

item.title: Where Should We Begin? with Esther Perel: I Want You To Want Me
item.description:
Couples often struggle with gaps in their sex drives, but what does a couple do when one person has no desire for sex whatsoever? A married couple comes to Esther with this question: one of them has recently discovered that she's asexual, while the other craves sex as a primary form of connection. Is theirs an irreconcilable difference? Is there hope for their future, or should they accept that divorce is the only option before them? Esther challenges their long-held assumptions about sexuality, and offers a third path forward.

item.title: Planet Money: Should we all be getting tariff refunds right now?
item.description:
Companies are getting billions of dollars back. How about us? 

It seems simple, right? We paid higher prices for imported goods because of tariffs. Then the tariffs were ruled illegal. Courts said the money paid to the U.S. government had to be refunded. Companies are getting that money now. 

It would seem like we, the customers, should get paid back, too. But … it’s not so simple. 

Once again, we’re dipping back into the drama of import tax law. We’re engrossed in the ups, downs, betrayal, and romance of … the Days of our Tariffs. 

In this edition:  “Refunds and Regrets.” 

How and why some companies and people are getting their IEEPA tariff refunds and other people are out of luck.

item.title: Radiolab: Math Vs Machine
item.description:
In less than four years, mathematician Steve Strogatz watched AI go from flailing at basic arithmetic to solving problems that baffle the world’s best mathematicians. In September of 2026, Open AI announced it had solved a Millennium Prize Problem, one of math’s highest achievements. In short, mathematics is right now on the cusp of a reckoning that may be coming for all of us. In this episode, Steve grapples with the idea that the window might be closing on humanity’s effort to unpuzzle, or learn, or understand the world around us.

Special thanks to Ravi Vakil, Alex Kontorovich, Bob Wright.

item.title: NerdWallet's Smart Money Podcast: Rebuild Your Credit And Your Savings, Plus Why 7 in 10 Americans Feel Squeezed
item.description:
Learn how to rebuild credit while saving in sinking funds, and why 7 in 10 Americans struggle to afford the basics.
How can you rebuild your credit and save for big goals at the same time? Hosts Sean Pyles, CFP, and Elizabeth Ayoola are joined by NerdWallet senior credit expert Amanda Barroso to answer a listener's question about moving from repairing bad credit to building excellent credit. They discuss which habits have the biggest effect on your score and how to spot errors on your credit report. They also cover when a secured credit card could make sense, how rent reporting and credit limit increases might help, and what credit score you typically need for a travel rewards card. Finally, they talk about how to set up sinking funds so the pursuit of credit card rewards doesn't turn into overspending.
Then, why are so many middle-class families struggling to afford the basics? Senior news writer Anna Helhoski talks with Lelaine Bigelow, executive director of the Georgetown Center on Poverty and Inequality, about their new Family Economic Well-Being Index. The index finds that 70% of Americans struggle to afford at least one basic need. They discuss why renters face heavier housing burdens than homeowners and why child care strains families even at higher incomes. They also get into why health care is the most widespread burden and how stacked costs can leave a family one surprise bill away from a crisis.

item.title: Song Exploder: Elvis Costello - Alison
item.description:
Elvis Costello is a singer and songwriter whose career spans five decades and over 30 albums. He’s a member of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and the Songwriter Hall of Fame. He’s won Grammy Awards, Ivor Novello Awards, a BAFTA, and he’s on Rolling Stone’s list of the greatest songwriters of all time. He put out his first album, My Aim Is True, in 1977. This month, he released a 49th anniversary edition of the album. So for this episode, I spoke to Elvis Costello about the making of “Alison,” from that debut album. Coming up, you’ll hear the isolated tracks from the original recording, as well as some additional parts that didn’t make the cut. And, in discussing the origin story of his song, we also ended up talking about the origin story of Elvis Costello himself.

For more info, visit songexploder.net/elvis-costello.
